topics.title: CPU Components & Control Unit Functions
topics.content:
CPU Overview:
- Serves as the central processing unit ('brain') executing instructions and directing operations.
- Main Components: Control Unit (CU), Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), and Registers.

Control Unit (CU):
- Manages and coordinates all hardware operations.
- Executes the Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle (Instruction Cycle).
- Control Memory: Stores microinstructions/microprograms used in microprogrammed control units to generate control signals.

topics.title: Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
topics.content:
Instruction Structure:
- Opcode (Operation Code) and Operand(s).
- Formats: Three-Address (ADD R1,R2,R3), Two-Address (ADD R1,R2), One-Address (Accumulator-based: ADD X), Zero-Address (Stack-based: ADD).

Addressing Modes:
- Immediate: Operand is specified directly in instruction (ADD R1, #5).
- Direct: Instruction contains the actual memory address.
- Indirect: Instruction points to a memory location containing the effective address.
- Register & Register Indirect: Operands reside in registers or register-pointed memory.
- Indexed: Effective Address = Base Address + Index Register.
- Relative: Effective Address = Program Counter (PC) + Offset.

topics.title: RISC vs. CISC Architectures
topics.content:
RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer):
- Simple, fixed-length instructions executing in single clock cycles.
- Uses Load/Store architecture and hardwired control unit for high-speed operation.
- Examples: ARM, MIPS, RISC-V.

CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer):
- Complex, variable-length instructions executing across multiple clock cycles.
- Rich set of addressing modes and microprogrammed control units.
- Examples: x86 (Intel, AMD).

topics.title: Pipelining & Parallel Processing
topics.content:
Pipelining:
- Overlaps instruction execution stages (Fetch, Decode, Execute, Memory, Write-Back) to increase instruction throughput.
- Pipeline Hazards: Structural (resource conflicts), Data (data dependencies), Control (branch/jump mispredictions).

Parallel Processing:
- Parallel execution paradigms: Instruction-Level (ILP), Thread-Level (TLP), Data-Level (DLP / SIMD), and Task-Level (MIMD).

topics.title: Arithmetic Operations & Signed Numbers
topics.content:
Arithmetic Operations:
- Integer Operations: Addition, Subtraction (via 2's complement), Multiplication (Booth's Algorithm), Division (Restoring/Non-Restoring).
- Signed Representations: 2's Complement is standard (Invert bits and add 1); eliminates dual-zero issues and simplifies addition/subtraction circuits.
- Overflow Detection: Signed overflow detected via XOR of Carry-in and Carry-out bits at MSB.

topics.title: Memory Hierarchy & Types
topics.content:
Hierarchy Levels (Fastest/Costliest to Slowest/Cheapest):
- Registers → Cache Memory (SRAM) → Main Memory (DRAM) → Secondary Storage (SSD/HDD) → Tertiary Storage (Tape/Cloud).
- Primary Memory Types:
  - SRAM: Fast, uses flip-flops, no refresh required; used in Cache.
  - DRAM: Slower, uses capacitors, requires periodic refreshing; used in Main Memory.
  - ROM/EEPROM/Flash: Non-volatile storage for firmware and persistent data.

topics.title: Cache Design & Operating Policies
topics.content:
Cache Mapping Functions:
- Direct Mapping: Memory block maps to exactly one cache line.
- Fully Associative Mapping: Block maps to any cache line (eliminates conflict misses).
- Set-Associative Mapping: Compromise mapping blocks into sets containing N ways.

Replacement Algorithms & Write Policies:
- Replacement: LRU (Least Recently Used), FIFO, LFU, Random.
- Write Policies: Write-Through (updates cache and main memory simultaneously) vs Write-Back (updates main memory only when block is replaced, uses dirty bit).

topics.title: I/O Modules & Data Transfer Modes
topics.content:
I/O Interface Methods:
- Programmed I/O (Polling): CPU continuously checks device status (wastes CPU cycles).
- Interrupt-Driven I/O: Device signals CPU when ready, freeing CPU for other processing.
- Direct Memory Access (DMA): Controller transfers data directly between I/O and RAM without continuous CPU intervention (Burst, Cycle Stealing, Transparent modes).

topics.title: Multiprocessor Systems & Interconnection Networks
topics.content:
Shared Memory Architecture:
- UMA (Uniform Memory Access / SMP): Equal memory access latency for all processors.
- NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access): Access latency varies depending on local vs remote memory.

Interconnection Structures:
- Shared Bus, Crossbar Switch, Mesh Networks, and Hypercubes.
- Cache Coherence & Synchronization: Maintains data consistency across caches using Mutexes, Semaphores, and Atomic operations.

subsections.title: HARDWARE-SOFTWARE DESIGN ISSUES ON EMBEDDED SYSTEMS

topics.title: Embedded Systems Basics & Classification
topics.content:
Overview:
- Microprocessor-based systems designed for specific dedicated tasks, often under strict real-time and power constraints.
- Classifications: Stand-alone, Networked, Mobile, Real-Time (Hard vs Soft Real-Time).

Components:
- Core Microcontroller (Arduino/ARM/PIC), Memory (Flash, RAM), I/O Interfaces (GPIO, ADC, DAC, PWM), and Communication Modules (UART, SPI, I2C).

topics.title: Custom Single-Purpose Processors & ASIPs
topics.content:
Single-Purpose Processors (ASIC):
- Hardwired logic for a single task; maximum performance and low power, but no flexibility.
- Optimization techniques: Pipelining, Parallelism, Hardware Sharing, Clock Gating.

ASIP (Application-Specific Instruction-Set Processor):
- Programmable processor with custom instructions tailored to specific domain applications (e.g., DSPs, GPUs).

topics.title: RTOS Concepts & Task Scheduling
topics.content:
RTOS Fundamentals:
- Guarantees predictable, deterministic execution under strict timing constraints.
- Concepts: Processes vs Threads/Tasks, Context Switching, Preemptive vs Cooperative Multitasking.

Scheduling Algorithms:
- Round-Robin, Priority-Based, Rate-Monotonic Scheduling (RMS - fixed priority based on period), Earliest Deadline First (EDF - dynamic priority based on deadline).

topics.title: Task Synchronization & Control Systems
topics.content:
Synchronization & Drivers:
- Mechanisms: Semaphores, Mutexes, Event Flags, Message Queues. Solves Race Conditions, Deadlocks, and Priority Inversion (via Priority Inheritance).

Control Systems:
- Open-Loop: No feedback, output does not affect control action (e.g., simple timer).
- Closed-Loop (Feedback): Compares output with desired setpoint to calculate error and apply adjustments (e.g., Thermostat, PID Controllers).

subsections.title: HARDWARE DESCRIPTION LANGUAGE AND IC TECHNOLOGY

topics.title: VHDL Structure & Data Types
topics.content:
VHDL Architecture:
- Entity: Declares the inputs and outputs (I/O interface).
- Architecture: Describes the internal logic, behavior, or structural design.

Data Types:
- std_logic (single bit values '0', '1', 'Z', 'X', etc.), std_logic_vector (multi-bit bus), integer.

topics.title: Combinational, Sequential Logic & IC Technology
topics.content:
Circuit Design in VHDL:
- Combinational Logic: Modeled using concurrent assignments (AND, OR, MUX, Decoders).
- Sequential Logic: Triggered by clock signals using PROCESS blocks (D Flip-Flops, Counters, FSMs).

IC Technologies:
- FPGA (Field Programmable Gate Array): Reconfigurable hardware logic.
- ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit): Fixed hardware fabricated for mass production.

questions.question: Which component is responsible for controlling the flow of instructions in a CPU?
questions.explanation: The Control Unit (CU) directs and coordinates all operations within the CPU.

questions.question: What type of memory is used for storing microinstructions?
questions.explanation: Control memory in a microprogrammed control unit holds sequences of microinstructions.

questions.question: Which addressing mode uses an offset added to a base address?
questions.explanation: Indexed Addressing computes effective address by adding an index register value to a base address.

questions.question: In an instruction format, what does the opcode field represent?
questions.explanation: The opcode specifies the exact machine operation (e.g., ADD, SUB) to be performed.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the Program Counter (PC)?
questions.explanation: The PC register holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched and executed.

questions.question: Which addressing mode specifies the operand value directly inside the instruction?
questions.explanation: In Immediate Addressing, the operand itself is included directly in the instruction field.

questions.question: What is RISC in computer architecture?
questions.explanation: RISC stands for Reduced Instruction Set Computer, designed for simple, fast execution.

questions.question: What is pipelining in CPU architecture?
questions.explanation: Pipelining executes multiple instructions simultaneously by overlapping their distinct execution stages.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of CISC architecture?
questions.explanation: CISC systems feature variable-length complex instructions that require multiple clock cycles.

questions.question: Which pipeline hazard occurs when two instructions attempt to access the same hardware resource simultaneously?
questions.explanation: Structural hazards arise due to hardware resource conflicts during overlapped execution.

questions.question: Which control technique uses fixed combinational logic circuits to generate control signals?
questions.explanation: Hardwired control units use fixed combinational logic circuits, providing maximum speed.

questions.question: What does the instruction ADD (R1), R2 signify in register indirect addressing mode?
options: Add contents of R1 to R2
Add value stored at the memory address in R1 to R2
Add immediate value in R1 to R2
Add memory address of R1 to R2
questions.explanation: (R1) means R1 contains the memory address of the operand to be added to R2.

questions.question: Which of the following refers to the organization of memory types based on speed, cost, and size?
options: Organization of memory types based on size only
questions.explanation: Memory hierarchy arranges storage devices from registers to secondary storage based on cost, capacity, and latency.

questions.question: Which type of memory is used to implement cache memory?
questions.explanation: SRAM (Static RAM) uses flip-flops, providing fast access without needing refresh cycles, making it ideal for cache.

questions.question: Which write policy ensures that write operations update both cache and main memory simultaneously?
questions.explanation: Write-Through updates both cache and main memory on every write to maintain data consistency.

questions.question: Which replacement algorithm evicts the block that has not been accessed for the longest time?
questions.explanation: LRU tracks access history and replaces the block that has been idle for the longest duration.

questions.question: What operation detects signed overflow in 2's complement addition?
options: XOR operation of carry-in and carry-out at MSB
questions.explanation: Signed overflow occurs when the Carry-into the MSB differs from the Carry-out of the MSB (detected by XOR).

questions.question: What does a 'dirty bit' in a cache system indicate?
options: Indicates whether a cache block is invalid
Indicates if the cache block has been modified
questions.explanation: In Write-Back cache systems, a dirty bit flags lines that have been modified locally and must be written to RAM upon replacement.

questions.question: Which mode of data transfer bypasses the CPU to transfer data directly to memory?
questions.explanation: DMA allows high-speed I/O devices to exchange data directly with main memory without invoking the CPU.

questions.question: What is 'cycle stealing' in DMA operations?
options: DMA controller temporarily halts CPU operations to access the memory bus
A processor steals instructions from main memory
Cache memory is locked during DMA transfers
Multiple instructions are executed in parallel
questions.explanation: In cycle stealing mode, DMA steals single bus cycles from the CPU to perform byte-by-byte transfers.

questions.question: Which technique ensures consistent data views across multiple caches in a multiprocessor system?
questions.explanation: Cache coherence mechanisms ensure that changes in one processor's cache are reflected across all other caches.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines an embedded system?
options: A general-purpose computer with external devices
A microprocessor-based system designed for a specific task
A system designed for cloud data storage
A desktop PC with high-speed RAM
questions.explanation: An embedded system is a dedicated computer designed to run specialized hardware/software for specific tasks.

questions.question: What is an Application-Specific Instruction-Set Processor (ASIP)?
options: To perform only basic arithmetic operations
A processor with instructions tailored for a specific domain
questions.explanation: ASIPs combine programmable CPU architectures with custom instruction sets tailored for specific application fields.

questions.question: Which optimization technique reduces dynamic power in single-purpose processors by disabling unused clock signals?
questions.explanation: Clock gating cuts off clock distribution to inactive logic blocks to minimize power consumption.

questions.question: Which scheduling algorithm assigns higher priorities to periodic tasks with shorter periods?
questions.explanation: Rate Monotonic Scheduling (RMS) uses static priority assignment proportional to task execution frequency.

questions.question: What type of control system uses feedback to compare actual output against a setpoint?
questions.explanation: Closed-Loop systems feed output measurements back to the input comparator to maintain target setpoints.

questions.question: What does VHDL stand for?
questions.explanation: VHDL stands for Very High-Speed Integrated Circuit Hardware Description Language.

questions.question: Which VHDL construct is used to describe the external interface (I/O ports) of a hardware design?
questions.explanation: The 'entity' block defines input/output ports and interface specifications of a VHDL component.

questions.question: Which VHDL construct is primarily used for modeling sequential logic circuits?
questions.explanation: Sequential logic statements execute inside a PROCESS block, which is triggered by sensitivity lists (e.g., clock edges).

questions.question: What is the main advantage of FPGAs over ASICs?
options: Lower unit cost for mass production
questions.explanation: FPGAs allow logic circuits to be reprogrammed and updated in the field, unlike fixed ASIC implementations.
